newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African navy wants ships and submarines.
newsitem.headline: South African navy wants ships and submarines.

text.p: South Africa's defence force on Wednesday asked parliament to approve the urgent purchase of four patrol corvettes and four second-hand British submarines.
Parliamentary defence committee chairman Tony Yengeni said his group would discuss the request "sooner rather than later" and told Reuters he expected a decision within two weeks.
Committee sources said they expected the package to be approved by the cabinet in time for inclusion in the March budget for fiscal 1997/98, probably by early November.

South African Navy Commodore Chubby Howell said the navy lost its last frigate in 1985 and told the committee that only four of the nine aging Israeli strike craft and none of its three French submarines were operational at present.
"We are looking at the survival of an arm of the service, let there be no mistake about that," he said.

He urged the committee to recommend to President Nelson Mandela's cabinet that South Africa should immediately revive a 1.7 billion rand ($375 million) programme to procure four corvettes, which are equivalent to European light frigates.

He said the programme, suspended last year in the face of widespread opposition to expensive defence projects, would meet the country's immediate surface requirement at a quarter of the cost of frigates.
Howell said the five shipyards shortlisted in the penultimate phase of the suspended acquisition process should be invited to submit new offers.
The successful bid would have to include countertrade proposals at least equal to the price of the ships, he said.
A defence department source at the meeting told Reuters the navy expected new offers to be at least 20 percent higher than the bids under discussion last year.
The search had been narrowed to Spain's Bazan shipyard, then considered the favourite, and Britain's Yarrow shipbuilders.

Howell suggested that shipyards in Denmark, Germany and France should be invited to make renewed offers, but said it would take too long and cost too much to extend the invitation to all 42 original bidders.
Howell also urged the committee to snap up a British Royal Navy offer of four Upholder class submarines in a package including training, spares and five years of logistical support.
He did not mention a price, but a secret military document shown to Reuters put the price at 2.07 billion rand, about a third of the estimated cost of four new submarines.
Chippy Shaikh, the defence department's director of logistics policy, said the navy should continue with a programme to refit its three aged Daphne class submarines and then put them up for sale.
He said that even with immediate approval, the British submarines, which would need to be recommissioned, would not be delivered until 1999.

Shaikh said the defence department would try to persuade the government to approve a package of submarines and corvettes, which could complement each other in the country's fight against rampant fish poaching and smuggling.
He told the committee that the navy requirements had been identified as the two most urgent projects out of a short list of seven defence areas needing urgent upgrades.
Others, on which decisions could be postponed until 1997, included the acquisitition of attack helicopters and army transport equipment. ($1=4.5 rands)
